The catalog records what is open. This is the attempt to close some of it: one study a
week, each aimed at a single entry, taken in priority order.

Scope is population-adjusted indirect comparison only, meaning MAIC, STC, ML-NMR, ML-UMR
and NMI. Standard network meta-analysis is out of scope because it does not adjust for
population differences, which is where these problems live.



## Completed

### [ADJ-04](problems/ADJ-04-flexible-outcome-surfaces-and-support-diagnostics-in-standar.qmd) — Weighted conformal prediction keeps its marginal guarantee under shift by returning infinite intervals where the source has no data

**Question.** Does weighted conformal prediction give valid intervals for target patients under covariate shift, including where the source has no data?

**Answer.** No. Weighted conformal intervals kept marginal coverage over the target (0.904 to 0.919 at nominal 0.9), but beyond the source's largest covariate value they covered 0.70 at a small shift and 0.83 at a moderate one, and at the largest shift they covered 0.99 only because 83% of those intervals were infinite. The method makes the support problem visible; it does not solve it. Estimating the density ratio changed nothing.

**What it does not answer.** Prediction intervals for individual outcomes rather than a marginal treatment effect; one covariate and one outcome model; no BART or Gaussian process arm; no support diagnostic scored as a classifier. Peer review has not been done.

### [ADJ-09](problems/ADJ-09-cross-environment-invariance-as-a-screen-for-bridges-and-mod.qmd) — An invariance screen for a bridging assumption, scored as a classifier

**Question.** Does instability across observed trials predict failure of a bridge used in a gap with no data, and does a screen on marginal effects fire under a valid bridge through non-collapsibility?

**Answer.** A stability screen across observed trials cannot confirm a bridge and refutes it rarely. With 4 or 10 trials, drift visible across them that biased the gap estimate by 0.28 was flagged in only 20% to 24% of analyses, and drift confined to the gap never above the null rate; passing the screen did not improve coverage of the reported analyses. Screening marginal log odds ratios raised false abstention under a valid bridge from 0.11 to 0.19 to 0.24 through non-collapsibility; screening conditional or standardized effects removed that.

**What it does not answer.** One event-rate level, no measurement shift, Cochran's Q only; environments valid by construction. Peer review has not been done.

### [ADJ-10](problems/ADJ-10-data-driven-modifier-and-causal-structure-discovery-with-few.qmd) — Modifier discovery across trials: no penalty is both stable and powerful, and study-level heterogeneity creates a false modifier that more trials entrench

**Question.** Are effect modifiers discovered from pooled trial data stable and correct enough to use, and do study-level confounders create false modifiers that more data do not remove?

**Answer.** No. Lasso discovery at the minimum-error penalty found the true modifiers but added 1.7 to 2.8 false ones among seven null covariates, and sets from independent datasets agreed with Jaccard similarity 0.37 to 0.57; the one-standard-error rule was stable only by selecting nothing (a single modifier found in 3% to 5% of analyses). With an unmeasured study-level cause of effect heterogeneity, pooled discovery selected the covariate whose trial means tracked it in 69% of analyses with 3 trials and 93% with 12 at the same total size, and raised false discoveries among the other covariates from 1.7 to 2.8 per analysis to 3.6 to 3.9; trial-specific treatment effects removed both.

**What it does not answer.** Lasso only (no multi-study causal forests); continuous outcome; linear modification; one overlap level; post-selection inference for the target not studied here. Peer review has not been done.

### [ADJ-15](problems/ADJ-15-privacy-guarantees-and-governance-for-shared-trial-level-dat.qmd) — Target moments released under differential privacy

**Question.** When a target trial releases covariate moments under differential privacy, how much does ignoring the added noise cost MAIC coverage at realistic arm sizes and budgets, does propagating its known variance repair it, and when do extra released moments stop paying for their share of the budget?

**Answer.** Privacy noise is not negligible at usable budgets for trial-sized targets: at epsilon 1 and 150 patients it was 8% to 60% of the estimate's variance and ignoring it cut coverage to 0.88 to 0.94; at 40 patients to 0.73. Its variance is known exactly, and adding it restored coverage in every scenario, conservatively where noise dominated. Releasing second moments pays only at larger budgets; at small ones it made MAIC infeasible in up to 87% of replicates.

**What it does not answer.** Laplace mechanism only; Gaussian mechanism, released correlations and overlap not varied. Results are conditional on feasible weights. Budget choice and governance are outside the study. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/ADJ-15-noise-whose-variance-is-known-exactly/out/ADJ-15.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/ADJ-15-noise-whose-variance-is-known-exactly/out/ADJ-15.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/ADJ-15-noise-whose-variance-is-known-exactly/out/ADJ-15.odt)

### [CMP-03](problems/CMP-03-strict-component-additivity-may-be-clinically-false.qmd) — An omitted component interaction biases never-administered regimens and leaks into regimens that do not contain it

**Question.** When additivity makes a never-administered combination estimable, how far can an omitted component interaction move its predicted effect, and does it contaminate other regimens?

**Answer.** No. At a synergy of 0.2 (twice a contrast's SE), 15 of 32 never-administered regimen results that the additive model reported as estimable had 95% coverage below 0.90, down to 0.11. Synergy on a never co-administered pair went wholly into the regimens containing it and was undetectable; synergy on a co-administered pair was absorbed into the component effects and biased regimens without that pair by -0.125, including a never-administered one. Modeling co-administered pairs' interactions removed the leakage. The share of a regimen's pairs never co-administered did not flag the failures (AUROC 0.37).

**What it does not answer.** One connected network, continuous outcome, fixed effect; no disconnection, covariate adjustment, selection procedures or formal synergy bound. Peer review has not been done.

### [CMP-12](problems/CMP-12-no-two-stage-adjusted-estimator-carries-multi-arm-covariance.qmd) — Splitting a multi-arm trial's adjusted contrasts is conservative for one contrast and anticonservative for another

**Question.** When a three-arm trial's population-adjusted contrasts share an arm and a weight vector, what is lost by treating them as independent, is the error ever anticonservative, and is dropping the trial cheaper?

**Answer.** Ignoring the within-trial covariance errs in a direction set by the contrast, not by how the arms' effect modification aligns. The trial's own B-versus-C interval became conservative in every scenario, while the network A-versus-B interval, which borrows through the trial, fell below nominal in 15 of 30 scenarios. The shared-weighting part of the covariance took both signs but never reversed a contrast's error. Dropping the trial widened the network interval by 29% to 91%.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome, linear modification, one three-arm trial in a fixed two-trial aggregate network; four-arm trials, the one-stage ML-NMR comparator and a bootstrap are not run, and target moments are fixed. Peer review has not been done.

### [CMP-13](problems/CMP-13-shared-gamma-conflates-within-and-between-study-modification.qmd) — Separating within-trial from across-trial component effect modification

Also bears on [IDN-06](problems/IDN-06-ml-nmr-interactions-can-rest-solely-on-aggregate-data-variat.qmd).

**Question.** Component ML-NMR fits one shared interaction on a globally centered covariate, which algebraically forces the causal within-trial interaction to equal the confounded across-trial association. How much does that cost, when, and is the damage really caused by aggregate data as the catalog claims?

**Answer.** Fitting one shared interaction matrix on a globally centered covariate is not pooling: for a binary modifier with study prevalence p_s it is algebraically identical to imposing that the causal within-trial coefficient equals the confounded across-trial one. In the model simulated, coverage of a nominal 95% interval for the causal interaction falls from 93.8% when that happens to be true to 17.2% when the two are equal and opposite, and further in networks whose contrasts move two components at once. Separating them costs about 5% in interval width and removes an order of magnitude of bias. The catalog's stated cause is incomplete: the loss is present with all twelve trials supplying individual data, so aggregate data are not necessary for it, but removing individual data roughly doubles the bias, so they amplify it.

**What it does not answer.** The registered global analysis is uninformative and the regime split that produced a usable answer was prompted by observing that failure, so it is not prespecified. The general headline about component ML-NMR is not established: the likelihood and nuisance structures are not mapped onto the fixed- and random-effect specifications the implemented method offers, and free study-by-treatment effects or priors can absorb or alter the term the identity isolates. A maximum-likelihood analogue of component ML-NMR. Implemented ML-NMR is Bayesian and priors matter most where interactions are weakly identified, so the coverage numbers do not transfer to multinma; the algebra does, and therefore so does the direction. One binary modifier, a log link, a Poisson outcome, additive components with no synergy, no random treatment-effect heterogeneity, no inconsistency, and exactly reported study prevalences. Under the discordance patterns the split model is correctly specified, so the study measures the cost of an algebraically known restriction rather than establishing that real networks contain within/across disagreement or how large it typically is. Continuous or multiple correlated modifiers, misspecified aggregate covariate distributions, and time-to-event outcomes are untested. It does not touch IDN-05.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/CMP-13-within-between-interaction/out/CMP-13.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/CMP-13-within-between-interaction/out/CMP-13.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/CMP-13-within-between-interaction/out/CMP-13.odt)

### [CMP-14](problems/CMP-14-aggregate-data-only-interactions-may-be-prior-driven.qmd) — Prior-to-posterior contraction and effective likelihood rank measure information, not bias

**Question.** CMP-14 asks for two default summaries, prior-to-posterior contraction per interaction and an effective likelihood rank, so an analyst sees when an aggregate-only interaction is held up by its prior. Would those summaries tell the analyst whether the reported interval covers?

**Answer.** Not reliably, and the reason is structural. On an exact identity-link arm of 504 scenarios and a logit arm of 72, no threshold on contraction, on either effective-rank reading, or on the estimability screen separates scenarios whose 95% interval covers nominally from those that fail. The summaries are functions of Fisher information and the prior, so within one design they are exactly constant while coverage ranges from 0 to 0.96. They partly catch the failure they were designed for: contraction flags 59% of failures caused by a tight prior. They catch none of the 142 failures caused by a biased route, where the ecological route carries between-study confounding or the additivity route a synergy, because confounding moves the posterior mean and not its information. A clean contraction says the likelihood spoke, not that it was right. Every result is exploratory.

**What it does not answer.** Nothing here is confirmatory: E1 was computed before its protocol existed, E2's separation rules were rebuilt after its output was read, and the cause decomposition was added for the manuscript. E1 is exact for a design realized at its quadrature nodes and E2 is asymptotic, so no posterior was sampled and neither is an average over realized designs. The exact invariance of the summaries holds for known-variance Gaussian models; with estimated variances or random effects they would move with a departure and whether that movement could ever warn is untested. One target component, one covariate, one network geometry, a normal within-study covariate law on the logit arm, and departures acting on the mean only. The protocol went through thirteen rounds of critique; the manuscript has not been peer reviewed.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/CMP-14-aggregate-only-interactions/out/CMP-14.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/CMP-14-aggregate-only-interactions/out/CMP-14.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/CMP-14-aggregate-only-interactions/out/CMP-14.odt)

### [CMP-15](problems/CMP-15-target-joint-covariate-distribution-is-only-approximately-kn.qmd) — Calibrating the correlation does not fix the copula: the family moves a standardized contrast by up to 0.03 on the log odds and log hazard scales

**Question.** Once a Gaussian copula's correlation is calibrated to the reported correlations, can the remaining error from copula family (asymmetry and tail dependence) move a target-standardized contrast?

**Answer.** Yes, modestly on the log odds and log hazard scales and strongly on the log rate scale. With margins and correlation matched, the calibrated Gaussian erred by up to 0.034 on the log odds ratio and 0.032 on the log cumulative hazard ratio (above 0.02 in 5 of 16 primary cells), with opposite signs for lower- and upper-tail dependence, and by up to 0.63 on the log rate ratio. The error plateaued by 256 integration points. A wrong flexible family was worse than the Gaussian in 61% of comparisons, so the defensible report is an envelope over families.

**What it does not answer.** Population-level; three exchangeable covariates with common margins; no mixed or discrete margins, vines or reconstruction uncertainty. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/CMP-15-the-copula-error-lives-above-the-second-moment/out/CMP-15.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/CMP-15-the-copula-error-lives-above-the-second-moment/out/CMP-15.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/CMP-15-the-copula-error-lives-above-the-second-moment/out/CMP-15.odt)

### [CMP-20](problems/CMP-20-poisson-aggregate-likelihood-needs-zero-exposure-rate-covari.qmd) — The aggregate Poisson likelihood is biased by the exposure-rate covariance, and exposure-weighted covariate moments remove the bias

**Question.** The aggregate Poisson likelihood multiplies an arm's total exposure by its mean modeled rate, which is exact only when exposure and rate are uncorrelated. The error is the factor 1 + rho CV(T) CV(lambda) per arm. How much bias does that put on a transported rate ratio at plausible levels of differential follow-up, and do exposure-weighted covariate summaries remove it?

**Answer.** No, the covariance cancels only when it is common to both arms. The bias followed the identity log{(1 + rho1 CV1(T) CV1(lambda)) / (1 + rho0 CV0(T) CV0(lambda))} (slope 0.994); at plausible dispersions with a differential correlation of at least 0.2, 27 of 64 cells had material bias or undercoverage, with bias up to 0.14 on the log rate ratio and coverage down to 0.17. Integrating aggregate arms over exposure-weighted covariate moments removed the bias everywhere (largest 0.008). Even with zero correlation the unweighted likelihood undercovered at large dispersions (0.84), because the finite-sample covariance is not zero.

**What it does not answer.** One covariate, one lognormal exposure law, no overdispersion, the same exposure mechanism in both studies; the likelihood is the study's own code, not multinma. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/CMP-20-poisson-exposure-rate-covariance/out/CMP-20.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/CMP-20-poisson-exposure-rate-covariance/out/CMP-20.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/CMP-20-poisson-exposure-rate-covariance/out/CMP-20.odt)

### [CMP-22](problems/CMP-22-ipd-availability-may-be-informative-rather-than-random.qmd) — Which trials supply individual data, and what selection on it does

**Question.** When the trials that supply individual data are selected on observed trial variables or on their own effect modification, how biased is the interaction evidence, does combining with aggregate trials help, and can a leave-IPD-out diagnostic reveal it?

**Answer.** Selection of which trials supply individual data on an observed trial variable caused no bias, but selection on the trials' own effect modification biased the within-trial interaction evidence by up to 0.14 (true 0.3), with coverage down to 0.59. Combining with the across-trial association in all trials halved the bias. A leave-IPD-out influence diagnostic did not respond to the selection, so the problem is invisible without a stated selection model.

**What it does not answer.** Pairwise continuous-outcome meta-analysis rather than component ML-NMR; no selection-model sensitivity analysis; one network size. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/CMP-22-measuring-the-dependence-before-modeling-it/out/CMP-22.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/CMP-22-measuring-the-dependence-before-modeling-it/out/CMP-22.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/CMP-22-measuring-the-dependence-before-modeling-it/out/CMP-22.odt)

### [CMU-02](problems/CMU-02-priors-not-data-can-drive-posteriors-in-weakly-identified-mo.qmd) — Do prior-sensitivity diagnostics catch the analyses that are actually wrong?

**Question.** In a population-adjusted network a proper prior yields a proper posterior even where the likelihood identifies nothing, so a narrow interval can reflect the prior rather than the evidence. The diagnostics that would expose this exist. What are their operating characteristics: do they flag the analyses whose intervals actually miss the truth, and how often do they cry wolf?

**Answer.** At the thresholds the literature suggests, they miss most of it. Pairing each warning with whether that replicate's own interval missed, a composite of four diagnostics has sensitivity 0.37 at a false-alarm rate of 0.16, falling to 0.13 outside two engineered geometries; the one sensitive rule fires on half the sound analyses too. Used as continuous scores the same statistics reach AUC 0.51 to 0.78, so this is a failure of thresholds rather than of the statistics. What no threshold repairs is that these diagnostics measure the prior's influence while the harm comes from the prior's location: with disconnected evidence and a tight prior four standard deviations from the truth, going from 100 to 400 per arm drops the warning rate from 0.98 to 0.01 while coverage stays near zero.

**What it does not answer.** The other half of CMU-02, wiring these diagnostics into released software, is untouched; neither multinma nor cpaic is run. The model is conjugate Gaussian with an identity link, a correctly specified linear mean and known variances, so nothing transfers directly to a non-conjugate posterior where MCMC error enters and the diagnostics behave differently. Only automated thresholds are evaluated; a plot read by an experienced analyst is a different instrument. Thresholds were taken from the source literature and not tuned. CMP-14 is touched only for the generic aggregate-only interaction, not for component models, and IDN-06 is not addressed at all because this design contains no within-versus-between discrepancy.

### [COV-02](problems/COV-02-no-evidence-on-how-the-modifier-set-changes-across-effect-sc.qmd) — The adjustment set is a property of the scale

**Question.** Does the set of covariates whose imbalance changes a transported contrast differ between the risk difference, risk ratio, marginal odds ratio and conditional odds ratio scales?

**Answer.** The covariates a transported contrast depends on change with the scale, but not in the nested way DESIGN.md predicted. Prognostic non-modifiers never affected the conditional log odds ratio and affected some marginal scale by more than 5% in 13 of 24 scenarios, the risk difference included, because with a logistic model every prognostic variable modifies the risk difference; the risk difference was in fact the most sensitive scale (median 4.5% change per unbalanced prognostic variable, against 1.6% for the marginal odds ratio). Sets differed between the risk difference, marginal and conditional odds ratio in 10 of 24 scenarios, below the registered threshold of half, so the refuting sentence holds as registered.

**What it does not answer.** No time-to-event scale; no sampling or estimation of the sets; independent normal covariates. Peer review has not been done.

### [COV-03](problems/COV-03-design-dependent-roles-of-prognostic-covariates.qmd) — What an anchored comparison must balance on a non-collapsible scale

**Question.** On the log odds ratio scale a purely prognostic covariate changes the marginal effect. Does an anchored MAIC that balances only covariate means, as practice does, leave material bias, and does balancing the variance of the prognostic index remove it at acceptable cost in effective sample size?

**Answer.** Yes. On the log odds ratio scale a difference in the spread of prognosis between trials biases an anchored MAIC that balances only means by up to 0.11, even with no effect modification. Balancing variances or the variance of the prognostic index removes the bias, but when the source is less dispersed than the target the loss of effective sample size makes RMSE worse than not balancing. G-computation was unbiased with the lowest RMSE throughout.

**What it does not answer.** Independent normal covariates and a correctly specified outcome model favor G-computation. Hazard ratios, skewed covariates and augmented estimators not run; MAIC intervals treat weights as fixed. Peer review has not been done.

### [COV-04](problems/COV-04-selection-uncertainty-in-paic-interaction-shrinkage-is-uncal.qmd) — Shrinkage priors on interactions do not give honest intervals for a transported effect

**Question.** Do posterior intervals from shrinkage or selection priors on treatment-by-covariate interactions keep frequentist coverage for the transported effect when the whole procedure is repeated?

**Answer.** No. Continuous shrinkage does not select, but its intervals still undercovered: 95% posterior intervals for the transported effect covered 0.794 to 0.948 with an empirical-Bayes ridge prior and 0.868 to 0.959 with a hierarchical normal prior, against 0.939 to 0.955 for a flat prior. When the interactions the target weights push the effect the same way, their joint shrinkage biases the transported effect (up to 0.19) and the narrower interval does not carry the bias. Integrating the prior scale recovers only part of the loss.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome with conjugate priors; no horseshoe, heredity constraints or projection-predictive selection; aligned modifiers only, no null scenario. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/COV-04-coverage-with-the-selection-step-included/out/COV-04.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/COV-04-coverage-with-the-selection-step-included/out/COV-04.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/COV-04-coverage-with-the-selection-step-included/out/COV-04.odt)

### [COV-09](problems/COV-09-measurement-non-equivalence-of-covariates-across-trials.qmd) — The same covariate name, two instruments

**Question.** When the source and target measure a matched effect modifier with different instruments, how is the MAIC estimate biased, does a reliability correction recover it, and can a bounded analysis over declared instrument differences contain the truth?

**Answer.** MAIC's bias from a modifier measured by different instruments follows a closed form in the instruments' offsets, slopes and the source reliability. A reliability correction removes it only when both trials use the same instrument; with differing instruments it left bias up to 0.18 and could undo a chance cancellation. An envelope of corrected intervals over declared instrument differences covered the truth at 1.4 to 2.9 times the naive width.

**What it does not answer.** Linear instruments and identity link only; misclassification of binary covariates and bridging-sample correction not run; target sampling error absent. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/COV-09-balancing-a-number-that-means-different-things/out/COV-09.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/COV-09-balancing-a-number-that-means-different-things/out/COV-09.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/COV-09-balancing-a-number-that-means-different-things/out/COV-09.odt)

### [COV-10](problems/COV-10-effect-modifier-selection-does-not-check-interaction-consist.qmd) — Interaction coefficients have their own consistency equation

**Question.** When direct and indirect paths carry opposing treatment-by-covariate interactions, does the pooled network meta-regression mask the modifier while the effect-consistency check passes, and can an interaction-consistency check detect it?

**Answer.** Opposing interactions on direct and indirect paths attenuate the pooled network meta-regression interaction toward zero, fully at the balance point and partly across a continuum, while the effect-consistency check stays at its null rate. The target effect was biased by 0.13 to 0.30 whether or not the covariate was selected. A direct interaction-consistency check detects it when studies per path and covariate spread are adequate (up to 1.00) and has little power otherwise (0.16 with two studies and narrow spread).

**What it does not answer.** Stylized triangles with continuous estimates; design-by-treatment interaction model and larger networks not run. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/COV-10-a-modifier-masked-while-the-consistency-check-passes/out/COV-10.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/COV-10-a-modifier-masked-while-the-consistency-check-passes/out/COV-10.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/COV-10-a-modifier-masked-while-the-consistency-check-passes/out/COV-10.odt)

### [COV-12](problems/COV-12-no-aggregate-integration-method-for-median-based-covariate-s.qmd) — Reconstructing a target covariate from a median: when the mean is enough and when it is not

**Question.** When a target publication reports a skewed covariate as a median with IQR or range, how much error does reconstructing its marginal put into a target-standardized contrast, and is that error a function of the reconstructed mean alone?

**Answer.** Under an identity link with linear effect modification, yes: the contrast error is exactly the modification coefficient times the mean error. Under a logit link, no: the mean explains only 60% of the error's variance, because the reconstruction's spread and shape also enter. With strong skew and a reported range, a normal reconstruction biased the contrast by more than 1 on the identity scale and 0.4 on the log odds ratio scale, growing with sample size; a lognormal matched to the reported quantiles kept bias below 0.1.

**What it does not answer.** One covariate with a known conditional model; estimated outcome models and multivariate marginals with dependence (CMP-15) are not covered. The lognormal matcher suits right skew only. ML-NMR integration is represented by direct integration. Two cells were run before a regressor correction and discarded unread. Peer review has not been done.

### [COV-14](problems/COV-14-per-comparator-adjustment-sets-yield-non-comparable-paic-con.qmd) — Covariate sets that differ across comparators, and the ranking read from them

**Question.** When one individual-data trial is compared with several aggregate comparators that report different covariates, does adjusting each contrast for everything it reports give a worse ranking than adjusting all contrasts for the common set, even though each contrast is less biased?

**Answer.** Neither adjustment rule protects the ranking. The common (intersection) set ranked better in 15 of 36 scenarios and the maximal sets in 19; which wins depends on whether the omission bias pushes a lower-ranked comparator past a higher one, which the data do not show. The registered inversion was not confirmed in the primary scenarios, whose pattern turned out to widen the top comparator's lead, but held in all six Fawsitt-like scenarios with similar populations. The intersection's per-contrast bias was a median 2.4 times the maximal. A bounded analysis over the other comparators' reported means covered at least 0.93 with similar comparator populations at little extra width.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome and independent covariates; non-collapsible outcomes, correlated omissions, a single ML-NMR network fit and overlap as a factor were not run. Three reporting patterns sample but do not exhaust where omissions can fall. Peer review has not been done.

### [DEC-01](problems/DEC-01-method-evaluations-score-estimator-error-not-decision-error.qmd) — Do estimation and decision rankings of population-adjustment methods agree?

**Question.** When population-adjustment methods are ranked by the decisions their estimates lead to rather than by RMSE, does the ranking change, and how does it depend on where the truth sits relative to the decision threshold?

**Answer.** For a threshold on a known side of the truth, yes: near the threshold in poor-overlap scenarios the RMSE and expected-loss rankings correlated at only 0.45, and the disagreement was reproducible, not noise. It came from the direction of bias: a biased method decided wrongly far less often when its bias pointed away from the threshold (0.11 against 0.64). Averaged over the two sides of the threshold, as an analyst who does not know the truth must, the rankings agreed (0.93, the same best method in every poor-overlap scenario). RMSE is therefore an adequate proxy for decision error unless the side of the threshold is known.

**What it does not answer.** Decision on the relative effect only, without a net-benefit model; one source of replicates (COV-03) and five methods; no ML-NMR; priors on the side of the threshold not modeled. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DEC-01-when-the-two-rankings-disagree/out/DEC-01.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DEC-01-when-the-two-rankings-disagree/out/DEC-01.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DEC-01-when-the-two-rankings-disagree/out/DEC-01.odt)

### [DEC-02](problems/DEC-02-no-factorial-study-ranks-which-choice-most-often-flips-a-dec.qmd) — Which analysis choice flips a decision

**Question.** Within one decision question, which analysis choices most often flip a population-adjusted recommendation, and how does that compare with the change in the question when the target population changes?

**Answer.** The choices are ordered rather than dominated by one. Near a decision threshold, adjusting or not flipped a population-adjusted decision in 36% of analyses, weighting against an outcome model in 20%, linear against quadratic STC in 13% and MAIC on means against means and SDs in 7%. Changing the target population moved the true log odds ratio by 0.39 to 0.59, more than any estimator choice moved the estimate, so the target belongs to the question, not the sensitivity analysis.

**What it does not answer.** No prior or bridge factor; decision on the relative effect only; one outcome type. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DEC-02-which-structural-choice-flips-a-decision/out/DEC-02.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DEC-02-which-structural-choice-flips-a-decision/out/DEC-02.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DEC-02-which-structural-choice-flips-a-decision/out/DEC-02.odt)

### [DEC-11](problems/DEC-11-intervals-omit-selection-reconstruction-and-target-summary-e.qmd) — Coverage of an STC interval after selecting effect modifiers on the same data

Also bears on [COV-01](problems/COV-01-deciding-which-covariates-are-true-effect-modifiers.qmd).

**Question.** When effect modifiers are selected on the analyzed data before an STC, does an interval that treats the selected model as fixed keep its coverage, and does resampling the whole procedure restore it?

**Answer.** Selecting effect modifiers on the analyzed data (interactions with p < 0.2) left the naive STC interval covering 0.887 to 0.927, because its SE ignored which model was selected; a bootstrap that repeats the selection restored 0.938 to 0.968. Lasso at the one-standard-error penalty dropped real modifiers and coverage fell to 0.33 with three modifiers at 1000 per arm. Fitting all candidate interactions kept coverage at 0.93 to 0.96.

**What it does not answer.** STC only; MAIC-based selection, overlap, larger candidate sets and target-summary uncertainty not run; 400 replicates. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DEC-11-selection-uncertainty-and-what-belongs-in-an-interval/out/DEC-11.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DEC-11-selection-uncertainty-and-what-belongs-in-an-interval/out/DEC-11.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DEC-11-selection-uncertainty-and-what-belongs-in-an-interval/out/DEC-11.odt)

### [DEC-28](problems/DEC-28-no-inference-is-reported-for-an-estimated-optimal-treatment-.qmd) — The covariate value at which the better treatment changes is often not estimable as a point, and borrowed precision can make its interval wrong

**Question.** Is the covariate boundary between two treatments' optimality well enough determined at achievable interaction precision to report as a point, and do standard intervals for it hold when interaction information comes partly from between-trial variation?

**Answer.** No. From one trial of 400 patients at a moderate interaction the exact (Fieller) 95% confidence set for the boundary was unbounded in 66% to 69% of replicates, while the delta-method interval was always finite and covered as little as 0.86 at the weakest interaction. Borrowing interaction precision from aggregate trials at different covariate means (81% of the precision) made the sets bounded, but a between-trial ecological term of 0.1 cut their coverage to 0.68 to 0.70 for a boundary away from the trials' mean covariate value. Treating by the point estimate at the moderate interaction lost 31% to 95% of the value of individualized treatment with one trial.

**What it does not answer.** Two treatments and one modifier; no modifier selection; closed-form frequentist estimators rather than ML-NMR; declared linear ecological term. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DEC-28-inference-on-the-optimal-treatment-boundary/out/DEC-28.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DEC-28-inference-on-the-optimal-treatment-boundary/out/DEC-28.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DEC-28-inference-on-the-optimal-treatment-boundary/out/DEC-28.odt)

### [DIA-02](problems/DIA-02-no-agreed-ess-definition-and-no-support-geometry-diagnostics.qmd) — The reported weight panel cannot see where support is missing

**Question.** Every member of the overlap panel MAIC reports (Kish ESS, ESS percentage, entropy efficiency, maximum weight, top-share) is a symmetric function of the weights, so none can depend on where in covariate space the source fails to cover the target. Does that blindness matter in an ordinary covariate law, or do weight concentration and support geometry move together tightly enough that the panel is an adequate proxy?

**Answer.** It matters. Two source populations that remove the same mass at the same threshold, one in the effect-modifying coordinate and one in a prognostic coordinate, give panels that agree to within 1.6% while one estimate is biased by 0.016 on the marginal risk difference and the other by less than 0.0001, and material error is 24 times as frequent in the first. Across the two placements every panel member sits within 0.005 of chance; region-specific ESS separates them almost perfectly and sliced optimal transport cost at 0.73, but a convex hull distance maximized over coordinates is as blind as the panel. The registered within-arm primary outcome reads the other way (panel 0.574, best geometric 0.592, rule returns refuted) because within one arm the hole placement is fixed and the outcome measures sampling noise, not geometry. Both readings are reported. Balance on the omitted moment, the comparator most likely to overturn the headline, was never fairly tested.

**What it does not answer.** Balance on the omitted moment, the free check registered as most likely to overturn the headline, was not tested: every cell where it had anything to see was removed by the matched-multiset control. Region-specific ESS was handed the easiest instance, since the region it examines is the region the hole empties, so its near-perfect separation is an upper bound; a hole in a high-modification region the analyst did not think to examine is untested and there it would fail like the panel. No diagnostic is calibrated to a threshold. The analysis subgrid was chosen by a mechanical rule written after the run was read. The realized high-modification hole holds 22% of the modification mass against a registered 25%. MAIC weights only, a binary outcome, normal covariates, one rectangular hole, good overlap only after the null control, and two of the three published ESS definitions. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DIA-02-the-whole-weight-panel-is-a-multiset-functional/out/DIA-02.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DIA-02-the-whole-weight-panel-is-a-multiset-functional/out/DIA-02.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DIA-02-the-whole-weight-panel-is-a-multiset-functional/out/DIA-02.odt)

### [DIA-03](problems/DIA-03-paic-diagnostics-are-not-evaluated-as-classifiers-of-realize.qmd) — Effective sample size tracks the error an analysis got by chance better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates

Also bears on [DIA-06](problems/DIA-06-failure-signatures-across-paic-estimator-families-are-unchar.qmd).

**Question.** Every population adjustment arrives with a panel of numbers beside it: effective sample size, the same figure as a percentage, the largest weight, standardized differences before and after adjustment, a distance between populations. A committee reads them as evidence about whether to believe the estimate, and a widely quoted rule says to worry below an effective sample size of about 30 to 35. Scored as classifiers of realized error, with discrimination and calibration, against known truth and under a declared distribution of analyses, what are they worth?

**Answer.** At the level at which a diagnostic is actually read, one analysis at a time, effective sample size tracks the error a study got by chance far better than the error it got from adjusting on the wrong covariates: AUROC 0.847 against the outcome-noise component and 0.813 against chance covariate imbalance between the source arms, both of which are functions of the covariates, the assignment and the weights, against 0.653 for the transport component that adjustment exists to remove. At the quoted cutoff of 35 it catches between a quarter and a third of material errors in every misspecification stratum, 0.309 where an effect modifier is omitted and the omission is diagnosable in principle, at specificity 0.926. No evaluated fixed cutoff met the registered requirement of sensitivity 0.80 at specificity 0.50 in every stratum. Three of the panel's members are provably one statistic, since ESS/n = 1/(1+CV^2(w)) exactly and area under the ROC curve is invariant to monotone transformation; a fourth, the post-weighting balance on matched moments, is zero at the solution of the calibration equations and among converged analyses cannot discriminate anything. On a decision-curve basis every rule in the panel is beaten by scrutinizing every analysis, up to an action threshold of 0.3.

**What it does not answer.** The second half of DIA-03 is untouched: no PSIS-LOO is computed at any hierarchical level and grouped study-level leave-one-out is no more implemented here than in the packages, so the mismatch between the level at which cross-validation is reported and the level at which the prediction is made remains open. DIA-06 is answered only in part; two estimator families and no adjustment are compared on identical replicates, but ML-NMR, NMI, doubly robust estimators and flexible learners are absent. The outcome is continuous with an identity link, which is what buys the exact error decomposition and is also the largest restriction: nothing here transfers to non-collapsible effect measures or time-to-event outcomes, where part of the error is a collapsibility artifact rather than an adjustment failure. Covariates are normal, comparisons are anchored, conditional constancy holds, and target moments are exact. The deployment weights are a declared judgment and nothing in this program measured them, which is why the primary results are within strata.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DIA-03-diagnostics-as-classifiers/out/DIA-03.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DIA-03-diagnostics-as-classifiers/out/DIA-03.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DIA-03-diagnostics-as-classifiers/out/DIA-03.odt)

### [DIA-07](problems/DIA-07-scenario-grids-omit-network-topology-and-information-placeme.qmd) — Where the individual data sit decides the error of a population-adjusted network contrast at the same total sample size

**Question.** At a fixed total sample size, does the error of a population-adjusted network contrast depend on the network's topology and on which trial supplies individual data, beyond total information?

**Answer.** No. At 1200 patients in every network, the probability of getting the sign of the decision contrast wrong ranged from 0.36 to 0.93 across four topologies and positions of the one individual-data trial (moderate modification, target shifted one SD), and the spread exceeded 0.10 in every scenario. An individual-data trial off every path to the contrast carried zero weight and changed nothing; standardizing one edge could raise the bias (0.20 to 0.30 in a line network) by removing an error that had offset the others.

**What it does not answer.** Deterministic calculation; continuous outcome, linear modification, four hand-built topologies, one IPD trial, fixed-effect model; no generated topology families, component networks or ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DIA-07-topology-decides-what-is-estimable/out/DIA-07.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DIA-07-topology-decides-what-is-estimable/out/DIA-07.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DIA-07-topology-decides-what-is-estimable/out/DIA-07.odt)

### [DIA-08](problems/DIA-08-paic-simulations-generate-only-shared-linear-effect-modifica.qmd) — Does the generator's effect-modification structure decide the method ranking?

**Question.** When effect modification departs from the shared linear form most simulations use, does the ranking of population-adjustment methods change?

**Answer.** Not at these magnitudes. The RMSE ordering under shared linear modification was reproduced under threshold, interaction and quadratic modification at every overlap level (rank correlation 0.9 to 1.0, the only change a swap between the two worst methods). STC with linear interactions ranked first everywhere even though the departures biased it by up to 0.12, because weighting methods lost more to variance at poor overlap. The generator decides a ranking only when a departure's bias exceeds the precision differences between methods.

**What it does not answer.** Moderate departure magnitudes only; treatment-specific, subnetwork and within-versus-between departures need a network and were not run; no ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DIA-08-generators-that-decide-the-comparison/out/DIA-08.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DIA-08-generators-that-decide-the-comparison/out/DIA-08.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DIA-08-generators-that-decide-the-comparison/out/DIA-08.odt)

### [DIA-09](problems/DIA-09-narrow-outcome-families-and-hazard-ratio-only-survival-scori.qmd) — Competing risks: a correct hazard ratio, a wrong cumulative incidence

**Question.** When population adjustment transports a time-to-event outcome with a competing cause, does a correctly transported cause-specific hazard ratio give the right cumulative incidence in the target, and what repairs it?

**Answer.** For competing risks, population adjustment transports the cause-specific hazard ratio (unbiased in every scenario) but not the cumulative incidence a decision model uses: when the target's competing hazard differed from the source's beyond the measured covariate, A's absolute incidence at 2 years was biased by up to 0.20 (true value 0.25) with coverage near zero. The between-arm difference was affected less. Recalibrating the competing hazard to the target's reported competing-event proportion removed the bias. The registered rule (bias beyond 0.05 wherever the competing hazard differed) was met in 20 of 24 method-scenarios; the exceptions were at half the competing hazard, with bias 0.041 to 0.049.

**What it does not answer.** Only the competing-risks family; cure fractions, recurrent events, ordinal and joint net-benefit outcomes not run. Exponential hazards, one covariate, no ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DIA-09-outcome-families-beyond-the-hazard-ratio/out/DIA-09.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DIA-09-outcome-families-beyond-the-hazard-ratio/out/DIA-09.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DIA-09-outcome-families-beyond-the-hazard-ratio/out/DIA-09.odt)

### [DIA-13](problems/DIA-13-qba-bias-mechanisms-are-not-crossed-with-the-primary-factors.qmd) — Do bias mechanisms in an unanchored MAIC combine additively?

Also bears on [QBA-22](problems/QBA-22-total-bias-is-non-additive-so-one-at-a-time-analyses-mislead.qmd).

**Question.** When an omitted confounder, comparator outcome misclassification and covariate measurement error act together on an unanchored MAIC, is their joint bias the sum of their separate biases, and does a one-at-a-time analysis bound it?

**Answer.** No. An omitted confounder and misclassification of the comparator's outcome interacted by up to 0.16 on the log odds ratio scale: with both at their largest the joint bias was about half the sum of the separate biases, and with the confounder reversed the joint bias had the opposite sign to that sum. Measurement error in a matched covariate combined nearly additively with either. The joint bias exceeded the largest single-mechanism bias in 22 of 36 combinations, so one-at-a-time analyses neither add up to nor bound it.

**What it does not answer.** Population-level only; no bias-analysis procedure, false reassurance or tipping sets; three mechanisms; selection and correlated parameters not varied. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/DIA-13-biases-that-act-together/out/DIA-13.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/DIA-13-biases-that-act-together/out/DIA-13.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/DIA-13-biases-that-act-together/out/DIA-13.odt)

### [DIA-14](problems/DIA-14-qba-is-judged-on-oracle-recovery-not-honest-classification.qmd) — A quantitative bias analysis verdict scored as a classifier

**Question.** How often does a QBA declare a MAIC decision robust when the true bias would reverse it, how does that depend on the elicited region rather than the method, and does oracle recovery reveal it?

**Answer.** A QBA's robust verdict is only as good as the elicited region. When the region contains the true bias the grid never reassures falsely (an exact property); with elicitation errors scaled to the region it reassured falsely at most 17% of the time the true bias reversed the decision, but with the common region centered at zero bias it did so 78%, 37% and 9% of the time at half-widths 0.05, 0.15 and 0.3. Probabilistic QBA avoided false reassurance by calling 62% to 85% of sound decisions fragile. Oracle recovery was nominal throughout and revealed none of this.

**What it does not answer.** One scalar bias parameter; effect modification and overlap not varied; the elicitation model is assumed. Peer review has not been done.

### [DIS-03](problems/DIS-03-baseline-risk-is-not-a-neutral-anchor-for-disconnected-evide.qmd) — A baseline-risk bridge across a disconnected network

**Question.** When disconnected subnetworks are linked through exchangeable baseline risks, does study-level design nuisance pass into the cross-gap contrast, and can design covariates separate it from prognosis?

**Answer.** A baseline-risk bridge transports whatever makes the subnetworks' baselines differ. When a design nuisance (such as an endpoint definition) coincided with the subnetwork it passed one for one into the cross-gap contrast (bias 0.2 to 0.7) and no adjustment was possible. When a quarter of trials used the other definition, adjusting for it removed the nuisance but not prognostic drift between subnetworks (bias 0.19 to 0.20).

**What it does not answer.** Study-level summaries, no Bayesian arm-based model or commensurate prior, one design covariate. Peer review has not been done.

### [DIS-11](problems/DIS-11-predictive-criteria-and-population-comparison-cannot-validat.qmd) — A predictive winner among models that share a false bridge

**Question.** When candidate models share a bridge assumption across a disconnected network, does a predictive criterion computed on observed trials rank them by their cross-gap error?

**Answer.** No. Candidate models that share the bridge had identical cross-gap bias (0 to 0.5 across scenarios), and the leave-one-trial-out winner was set by within-subnetwork structure: meta-regression won when a trial covariate changed the contrast, the common-effect model when not, with the same distribution at every bridge error. A predictive criterion on observed trials cannot rank models by an error they share.

**What it does not answer.** Frequentist predictive densities rather than LOO-PSIS on ML-NMR; no grouped leave-subnetwork-out or synthetic deletion; population comparison not simulated. Peer review has not been done.

### [DIS-21](problems/DIS-21-match-acceptance-thresholds-are-uncalibrated-against-bridge-.qmd) — A matched bridge's admission threshold sets its bias: at the threshold used in practice the bridged contrast was biased by twice the true effect

**Question.** How do the bias of a matched bridge across a disconnected network and the existence of the bridged comparison depend on the admission threshold, expressed in multiples of the distance between arms of one randomized trial?

**Answer.** No. With trial populations shifted across the gap, the bridged contrast (truth -0.2) was biased by -0.03 at the within-trial arm distance, where the bridge existed in only 8% of replicates, -0.13 at three times it and -0.44 at ten times it, near the threshold used in practice, where it always existed and its interval never covered. An index omitting the most prognostic covariate was biased by -0.25 even at the tightest threshold. Pooling pairs that reuse arms made intervals undercover even without bias (0.76 at ten units with good overlap).

**What it does not answer.** Monte Carlo networks only, no real-network deletions; one distance with two covariate sets; no component network meta-analysis bridge; admitted pairs pooled as independent. Peer review has not been done.

### [EST-06](problems/EST-06-the-maic-paradox-swapping-the-ipd-trial-can-reverse-the-comp.qmd) — When two sponsors' MAICs disagree: how often, why, and which common target resolves it

**Question.** When two sponsors run MAIC on the same two trials, each weighting its own data to the other trial, how often do their conclusions reverse, how much of that is a real difference in target population rather than sampling error or differing adjustment sets, and which common-target remedy recovers the decision population's effect?

**Answer.** Reversal is mostly a real target difference and it is common: with the modifier's zero-effect point between the two populations, sponsors disagreed in sign in 23% to 56% of analyses at separations up to 1 SD and modification up to 0.4, and moving the point outside the populations cut that by a median 0.31. The two sponsors' estimates are correlated, which a reversal calculation must use. Under linear modification the plain average of the two analyses is as accurate for the midpoint population as transporting both trials there.

**What it does not answer.** Linear modification and a continuous outcome; with nonlinear modification or a non-collapsible scale the average is not the midpoint effect. The arbitrated indirect comparison and measurement differences between trials were not run. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/EST-06-maic-reversal-region/out/EST-06.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/EST-06-maic-reversal-region/out/EST-06.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/EST-06-maic-reversal-region/out/EST-06.odt)

### [EST-12](problems/EST-12-treatment-hierarchies-lack-a-declared-target-population-refe.qmd) — Treatment hierarchies across target populations

**Question.** Does a treatment hierarchy move more across plausible target populations than across sampling variability, so that a hierarchy must name its population?

**Answer.** Yes: where effect modification changed the true ranking across plausible targets, the estimated hierarchy moved 1.6 to 2.4 places per treatment across targets against 0.1 to 1.4 places across sampling replicates, so a hierarchy must name its population. But estimated hierarchies also moved 0.2 to 2.1 places across targets where the true ranking did not change, through the uncertainty of meta-regression slopes away from the data's center, so a changed hierarchy is not by itself evidence of population dependence.

**What it does not answer.** Study-level meta-regression rather than ML-NMR; P-scores only; one covariate; fixed-effect. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/EST-12-a-hierarchy-with-no-population/out/EST-12.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/EST-12-a-hierarchy-with-no-population/out/EST-12.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/EST-12-a-hierarchy-with-no-population/out/EST-12.odt)

### [HET-02](problems/HET-02-multi-arm-covariance-is-lost-when-contrasts-are-adjusted-pai.qmd) — Matched single-arm studies built against one comparator arm

**Question.** When several single-arm studies are each matched to the same comparator arm and their pseudo-contrasts enter a network as independent, how much does that overstate precision, and does it change the conclusion?

**Answer.** Entering pseudo-contrasts built against one comparator arm as independent counts that arm once per study. Its reported SE shrank as studies were added while the estimate's spread did not, so coverage fell from 0.88 with one study to 0.57 with eight (comparator arm of 50). Modeling the shared covariance kept coverage at 0.95. In this fixed-effect network the point estimate barely changed; the error is in the stated precision.

**What it does not answer.** Fixed-effect continuous network without a weighting step; heterogeneity and conflicting evidence, where the point estimate can also move, not run. Peer review has not been done.

### [HET-04](problems/HET-04-node-splitting-compares-paths-without-standardizing-to-a-tar.qmd) — A population difference arriving as inconsistency

**Question.** When the studies supplying the direct and indirect paths of a loop differ in an effect modifier, how often does unadjusted node splitting flag the population difference as inconsistency or miss a real conflict that the difference cancels, and what does an adjusted split achieve?

**Answer.** Unadjusted node splitting tests inconsistency plus population mismatch. With no true inconsistency it flagged 14% to 98% of analyses when the direct and indirect study sets differed in an effect modifier, and it fell to its null rate when the mismatch cancelled a real conflict. A split adjusted for the modifier held size (4% to 6%) and recovered some masked conflicts, but its precision fell as the gap between the study sets grew.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous study estimates, one loop, no Bayesian node split or marginalization to a named target. Peer review has not been done.

### [HET-10](problems/HET-10-no-calibrated-small-study-interval-method-for-population-adj.qmd) — Interval coverage for population-adjusted synthesis with few studies

**Question.** How does interval coverage of population-adjusted random-effects synthesis depend on the number of studies, when one individual-data trial supplies the adjusted contrast for several aggregate trials?

**Answer.** Coverage fails in two ways. Meta-analyzing per-trial adjusted contrasts that reuse one individual-data trial as if independent lost coverage as trials were added (down to 0.55 at twelve trials with DerSimonian-Laird), because the shared error does not average out. Pooling the aggregate trials first and subtracting the transported contrast once fixed that; with DerSimonian-Laird it stayed within 0.93 to 0.97 from four trials, and Hartung-Knapp was conservative (up to 1.00) at two or three.

**What it does not answer.** Pairwise synthesis with one individual-data trial; continuous outcome; no one-stage or Bayesian analysis; one overlap level. Peer review has not been done.

### [IDN-01](problems/IDN-01-transitivity-and-conditional-constancy-cannot-be-tested-in-s.qmd) — What each transitivity screen can see

**Question.** Do the available transitivity screens (covariate dissimilarity, loop inconsistency, heterogeneity), run together, detect the violations that bias a network estimate, and can their pattern of flags identify the mechanism?

**Answer.** No. Each screen sees one direction of violation, and an unmeasured modifier that makes one treatment look better in every comparison that includes it is invisible to all three: at size 0.4 it biased the network estimate by 0.40 with coverage near zero while the screens together fired at their null rate (0.28). Loop breaks and drift were detected with power rising in the number of studies, but the pattern of flags identified the mechanism poorly, and a measured modifier was always flagged although adjustment removed its bias.

**What it does not answer.** Stylized triangle networks with continuous estimates; calendar drift as random shifts; abandonment records not scored. Peer review has not been done.

### [IDN-05](problems/IDN-05-the-shared-effect-modifier-check-has-low-and-uncalibrated-po.qmd) — A violation twice the size that would change a decision raises the shared effect modifier check's alarm rate from 1.3% to 4.5%

**Question.** Population adjustment across a network assumes that a covariate modifies the effect of every active treatment in a class in the same way. There is one published within-network check on that assumption: fit the model with a single interaction shared across the class, refit with treatment-specific interactions one covariate at a time, and compare the posteriors and the model fit. Its authors say it likely has low power. Nobody has measured it, there is no threshold that separates a pass from a failure, and there is no statement of what a pass licenses. Scored against a known truth under a declared distribution of networks, what is it worth?

**Answer.** The check does not have the resolution to test the assumption it is read as testing. Against a violation already twice the size that would change a decision, the DIC rule fires in 0.045 [0.029, 0.070] of analyses, against 0.013 [0.005, 0.029] when the assumption holds exactly: a violation that doubles the error that matters moves the alarm rate by about three percentage points. The result does not depend on where the cut is put. Scored threshold-free, the DIC difference ranks a violated network above an intact one with an AUROC of 0.557 [0.517, 0.596] at that violation, so no threshold recovers a ranking the statistic does not contain. The posterior standard deviation of the interaction contrast runs 0.30 to 1.64 against the 0.153 that would make a transported estimate materially wrong, which is why. The equivalence reading, the only one that could confirm rather than merely fail to contradict, fired zero times in 3,200 opportunities, including every replicate where the assumption held exactly; that is a statement about precision, and partly about the prior, since independent normal(0, 2.5) priors already place 0.965 of the contrast beyond the margin. Following the check is still better than not: relaxing exactly what it fires on beats relaxing everything at every target displacement and beats imposing the restriction at every displacement except zero, where the two are indistinguishable.

**What it does not answer.** The design is a best case in several specific ways that favour the check, and failures attributable to those idealizations are conservative; no general lower-bound claim is made, because three features cut the other way. The true marginal reference risk in the target is supplied to the estimator. Covariates are normal with known target moments and study covariate means are drawn independently of study baselines and of the random treatment effects, so the ecological route identifying the aggregate-only treatment's interaction is unbiased by construction. Conditional constancy holds and only one covariate drifts, linearly. Against that: the fits are fixed-effect while half the cells generate random treatment effects, which is a second specification error that inflates firing; the likelihood is integrated over 64 quadrature points and refitting at 256 changes the DIC verdict in 8.3% of a 24-network subset, which is noise belonging to the implementation and not to the evidence, and 256 points is not demonstrated to be converged; and a single individual-level study is an assumption about the network rather than necessarily a pessimistic one. Beyond that: what a second individual-level study would buy is not measured, that factor having been dropped to pay for treatment-effect heterogeneity. With two active treatments and two covariates, multiplicity across covariates and the selection involved in reading the widest of several pairwise differences are not measured. Where treatment-effect heterogeneity is present the estimand is not cleanly defined, since truth is set at a random effect of zero while a fixed-effect model targets a function of the realized studies; primary results are repeated on the sixteen homogeneous cells and do not change. The hierarchical middle ground between shared and independent interactions could not be fitted because the package does not implement it, and we did not implement it ourselves: that is a reason for its absence, not a justification. The five decision rules scored here are our formalizations of an exploratory published practice, not published rules, and their operating characteristics are ours. Fifty replicates per cell gives a per-cell standard error of 0.065, so nothing is read off a single cell.

### [IDN-07](problems/IDN-07-no-agreed-criterion-for-when-a-held-out-trial-discrepancy-fa.qmd) — Calibrating a held-out-trial falsification rule

**Question.** When one trial is withheld and its contrast predicted from the rest, which pass or fail rule holds its type I error, how much power does it have, and what does omitting a variance component or mis-targeting the prediction do?

**Answer.** A held-out-trial check has a controllable size if the prediction targets the withheld trial's own population and its variance includes between-trial heterogeneity: the full rule's size was 0.035 to 0.073 (registered limit 0.07, exceeded by 0.003 in one scenario). Omitting heterogeneity raised size to 0.104, and aiming the prediction at the remaining trials' population raised it to 0.96. Power against a violation as large as the effect was only 0.21 to 0.47, so a pass licenses very little.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome and G-computation only; no MAIC weight variance, no Bayesian predictive or conditional-moment rule; five aggregate trials. Peer review has not been done.

### [IDN-09](problems/IDN-09-negative-controls-for-itc-lack-catalogues-power-and-calibrat.qmd) — A negative-control outcome for transport bias

**Question.** Can a negative-control outcome detect and calibrate transport bias in an unanchored MAIC, and when does the calibration fail?

**Answer.** Only in a knife-edge case. A negative-control outcome with no treatment effect detects a population difference (flag rate up to 0.83) but calibrates the primary contrast correctly only when its dependence on the unmeasured covariate equals the primary outcome's and that covariate does not modify the treatment effect (bias 0.001). Otherwise the calibrated contrast was biased by -0.18 to 0.40: it missed the modification part, overcorrected with a more strongly dependent control, and cancelled by coincidence in one scenario.

**What it does not answer.** One control outcome rather than a bank with empirical calibration; unanchored only; availability of control outcomes not surveyed. Peer review has not been done.

### [IDN-10](problems/IDN-10-transported-control-arm-outcomes-are-uncalibrated-where-it-m.qmd) — A transported control-arm check carries no information about the anchored contrast

**Question.** Does agreement between a MAIC-transported control arm and the target's observed control arm tell an analyst whether the anchored relative effect is biased?

**Answer.** No. The check tests prognostic transport, which an anchored contrast does not need, and cannot see effect-modification transport, which it does. A prognostic shift raised the alarm rate to 0.48 while the contrast was nearly unbiased (bias -0.03 to -0.06); a modifier shift biased the log odds ratio by 0.30 with the alarm rate at 0.044. Pooled over 18,000 analyses the check's AUROC for a biased contrast was 0.50.

**What it does not answer.** Binary outcome only; survival-curve and RMST versions, unanchored comparisons, offsetting prognostic mechanisms and outcome-definition or follow-up differences are not simulated. Peer review has not been done.

### [MIS-01](problems/MIS-01-missing-aggregate-summaries-and-unavailable-ipd-have-no-reme.qmd) — Missing covariate values in the individual-data trial of a MAIC

**Question.** When a matched covariate is missing for some patients in the individual-data trial, when is complete-case MAIC biased, and do inverse-probability-of-observation weighting and multiple imputation repair it?

**Answer.** Complete-case MAIC bias is set by the missingness mechanism, not the rate. It is unbiased when missingness depends only on matched covariates, including the missing covariate itself, and biased already at 15% missingness when it depends on an unmatched effect modifier, the outcome with modification, or an unmatched covariate in one arm only. Weighting and imputation repair the missing-at-random cases (imputation with arm interactions most reliably) but are biased by up to 0.22 when missingness depends on the missing covariate itself, where complete case is not.

**What it does not answer.** Missing outcomes, binary outcomes, STC, overlap levels and pattern-mixture sensitivity analysis not run; single-driver mechanisms only. Peer review has not been done.

### [MIS-03](problems/MIS-03-nothing-propagates-sampling-error-in-reported-target-moments.qmd) — What conditioning on sampled target moments costs

Also bears on [EST-07](problems/EST-07-reported-target-moments-are-treated-as-known-constants.qmd).

**Question.** Population adjustment treats a target trial's published covariate means and standard deviations as exact, though they are sample estimates. By how much does that cost interval coverage at realistic sample sizes, and what would a publication have to report for a correction to work?

**Answer.** Two things, established by different means. Analytically: the variance a standard interval omits is (1-2k)Var_T(tau)/n_T to first order, where k is how far the target trial's own treatment effect is modified by the same covariates as the source trial's, so the sign is set by a quantity the usual inputs do not identify; and a correction adding only the positive term is closer to the right variance than doing nothing only when k < 1/4. Empirically, and only in an exploratory subset: the omission runs from 9.5% too much variance to 14.9% too little and moves coverage between 92.1% and 96.2%. The registered analysis is uninformative and the confirmatory coverage question remains open.

**What it does not answer.** The registered coverage question is not confirmatorily answered: every usable coverage result comes from a post-run restriction conditioning on an observed outcome. One estimator, one outcome type, one information structure. Covariates are multivariate normal, which is also the assumption the deployable correction is derived under, so it is measured under conditions favorable to it; skewed, bounded and categorical covariates are untested. The outcome is continuous and the effect additive, so marginal and conditional effects coincide, and nothing transfers directly to binary or time-to-event outcomes, where MAIC is most used. Effect modification lies exactly in the span of the matched moments, so this is a variance result under correct identification and says nothing about bias. The target moments and the target treatment effect come from the same trial, which is the common case but not the only one. STC, ML-NMR, ML-UMR and NMI have different sensitivities and are not covered. EST-07's other components, model uncertainty in reconstructed correlations, inclusion-criteria ambiguity and secular drift, are not sampling error and are untouched. The alignment parameter imposes exact non-negative proportionality between source and target modifier coefficients, so modifier sets differing in direction or overlapping only partially are untested.

### [MIS-04](problems/MIS-04-model-and-bridge-selection-uncertainty-never-enters-the-inte.qmd) — Choosing among population-adjustment models on the same data

Also bears on [MOD-04](problems/MOD-04-no-post-selection-inference-for-model-choice-in-population-a.qmd).

**Question.** When the adjustment model is chosen from the analyzed data, does the chosen model's interval keep its coverage, and what does averaging over candidates change?

**Answer.** For choices among MAIC and STC specifications the candidates are close: choosing the most precise method covered 0.938 to 0.956, like a prespecified one. Choosing the most favorable estimate shifted it by up to 0.26 on the log odds ratio scale while its interval still covered 0.927 or more, because the favored method often had a wide interval. Averaging with between-model variance over-covered (up to 0.991) because the candidates share data; that difference makes the refuting sentence fail as registered.

**What it does not answer.** Outcome and weighting models only; treatment partitions and bridges not studied; equal weights. Peer review has not been done.

### [MOD-15](problems/MOD-15-no-calibrated-rule-says-when-within-and-across-trial-interac.qmd) — The half-standard-error pooling rule for interactions is stated in the wrong standard error

**Question.** The published rule pools within-trial and across-trial interaction estimates when they differ by less than half the across-trial standard error. What are its pass rate, the bias and coverage of what it reports, and how does it compare with a test stated in the difference's own standard error?

**Answer.** The difference's standard error is sqrt(sW^2 + sA^2), not sA, so under equality the rule pools with probability at most 0.383 (0.31 to 0.37 in the networks studied): it refuses valid pooling most of the time in every regime. When it pools under ecological bias, the pooled interval can cover as little as 22%. Its RMSE matches never pooling to within 0.3%, forgoing the 2% to 19% gain pooling offers when the estimates agree.

**What it does not answer.** Independent normal estimates with known standard errors; no between-trial heterogeneity; all trials with individual data. The ML-NMR case, where aggregate trials inform only the across-trial component, is not computed. No agreement rule can detect trial-level confounding that is small relative to the across-trial standard error. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/MOD-15-a-rule-stated-in-the-wrong-standard-error/out/MOD-15.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/MOD-15-a-rule-stated-in-the-wrong-standard-error/out/MOD-15.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/MOD-15-a-rule-stated-in-the-wrong-standard-error/out/MOD-15.odt)

### [MOD-16](problems/MOD-16-no-criterion-chooses-pooled-or-arm-separate-matching-in-anch.qmd) — Arm-separate matching cancels the aggregate trial's chance imbalance; pooled matching carries it

**Question.** Arm-separate matching weights each individual-data arm to the corresponding aggregate arm; pooled matching uses one weight function. When does each give a biased anchored comparison, and is the bias of arm-separate matching the product of unmatched prognostic strength and aggregate arm imbalance, as the design claims?

**Answer.** The product claim is wrong. Given an aggregate-trial imbalance kappa, pooled matching is biased by kappa (beta/2 + gamma_X + gamma_U rho_T) and arm-separate matching by kappa gamma_U (rho_T - rho_S); simulation matched both (slopes 1.00 and 0.96). Arm-separate matching reproduces the aggregate imbalance in the individual-data contrast so it cancels, and is biased only when an unmatched prognostic covariate relates to the matched one differently in the two trials. It had smaller bias than pooled matching in every scenario with an imposed imbalance and 10% to 27% lower RMSE under chance imbalance.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome, linear model, one matched and one unmatched covariate, shared effect modification; the non-collapsible case, where arm-separate matching compares arms in different populations, is not studied, and the arm-separate interval's conservatism is not repaired. Peer review has not been done.

### [MOD-18](problems/MOD-18-risk-modeling-network-meta-regression-treats-a-fitted-risk-s.qmd) — An estimated risk score used as a regressor

**Question.** When a risk score estimated in a prognostic cohort is used as a regressor for treatment-effect heterogeneity, does treating it as data understate the interval, and is the understatement worst at the tails of risk?

**Answer.** Little, given a prognostic cohort of about a thousand patients or more: propagating the score's estimation uncertainty widened intervals by at most 2.4%, and plug-in coverage stayed near nominal. With 300 cohort patients the widening reached 7% at the risk tails against about 1% at the median, confirming that the understatement is worst where recommendations are made, and plug-in coverage fell to 0.924. The registered rule (plug-in coverage at least 0.93 everywhere) was missed in that one scenario, so the refuting sentence fails as registered.

**What it does not answer.** Pairwise six-trial analysis; frequentist bootstrap rather than a joint or cut Bayesian model; well-specified score. Peer review has not been done.

### [OUT-02](problems/OUT-02-rare-events-separation-and-zero-event-studies-in-weighted-sy.qmd) — Effective sample size counted in events: right direction, no gain over ESS times the event rate

**Question.** With rare binary outcomes, does an effective sample size counted in events (EESS) predict when a MAIC interval fails better than the reported ESS multiplied by the event rate, and in which direction do the two diverge?

**Answer.** EESS is the reciprocal of the sandwich variance of a weighted log odds, and it differs from ESS times the event rate by E_w[w]E_w[p]/E_w[wp]: below 1 when weights concentrate on high-risk patients, above 1 on low-risk ones (the design had the direction reversed). As a predictor of failure the two were equivalent (AUROC 0.839 and 0.858) and ESS alone was poor (0.662). Their predictive value comes from zero-event analyses; once an estimate exists, non-coverage is near nominal and neither predicts it.

**What it does not answer.** One prognostic covariate, MAIC on means; the penalized, Firth, Bayesian and fail-closed estimators were not run, and unanchored comparisons and multivariable separation are outside the design. Peer review has not been done.

### [OUT-05](problems/OUT-05-unequal-variances-skew-and-bounded-scales-in-continuous-outc.qmd) — The transported mean is safe and the responder probability is not

**Question.** When a bounded continuous outcome is transported by G-computation with a pooled normal residual, is the mean contrast safe while the responder-probability contrast is biased, and does a floor make the bias depend on the target population?

**Answer.** Yes. With a pooled normal residual the transported mean contrast was unbiased while the responder-probability contrast was biased by up to 0.10 when the arms' dispersions differed, with opposite signs at a threshold near the median and one in the tail. Arm-specific SDs fixed it only for normal errors without a floor; Tobit fixed the floor but not skew; logistic regression of the responder indicator was unbiased everywhere. A floor biased the mean contrast by under 2% of the effect, somewhat more at the larger target shift.

**What it does not answer.** One source trial, no ceiling, no intervals, no ML-NMR. Peer review has not been done.

### [OUT-06](problems/OUT-06-change-scores-trajectories-and-responder-threshold-estimands.qmd) — Change scores and endpoints do not diverge under population adjustment

**Question.** When baseline severity modifies the treatment effect, do change-score and endpoint analyses give different target-population contrasts after population adjustment, in proportion to the product of the interaction and the baseline shift?

**Answer.** No. Baseline is pre-treatment, so the target follow-up and change contrasts are one quantity under any adjustment. Across 24 scenarios, MAIC and G-computation never diverged beyond Monte Carlo error, and were identical to machine precision in unanchored comparisons. The only divergence was in naive unanchored comparisons, equal to 1.00 times the baseline shift and independent of the baseline-by-treatment interaction.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome with a linear conditional mean only; nonlinear links, threshold-based responder estimands and joint repeated-measures models are not tested. Peer review has not been done.
