### [OUT-07](problems/OUT-07-informative-censoring-and-outcome-dependent-missingness.qmd) — Informative censoring on the two sides of an indirect comparison

**Question.** When censoring depends on latent risk in the source and comparator trials to different degrees, does the bias cancel in the indirect RMST contrast, what does source-side IPCW achieve, and does a one-sided comparator sensitivity analysis cover the truth?

**Answer.** Informative censoring cancels in an indirect RMST contrast only when the two mechanisms match. Unanchored, with differing mechanisms the bias was -2.3 to +1.4 months against a true difference of 0.62, reversing the comparison in up to 97% of analyses; equal mechanisms nearly cancelled. Anchored comparisons were protected (bias within 0.22) because both arms of each trial shared its mechanism. Adjusting only the source by inverse probability of censoring weighting helped partly where only the source was informative and broke the cancellation where both were.

**What it does not answer.** No covariate shift between trials; time-constant censoring hazards; one sensitivity parameterization; one baseline proxy. Peer review has not been done.

### [OUT-08](problems/OUT-08-overdispersed-counts-and-recurrent-events-as-total-disease-b.qmd) — Overdispersed and zero-inflated counts transported by G-computation

**Question.** For count outcomes transported to a target, does overdispersion bias the estimate or only its interval, and when the fraction of structural zeros differs between populations, what does a count model transport wrongly and what repairs it?

**Answer.** Overdispersion leaves the transported rate ratio unbiased and makes the Poisson interval too narrow (coverage down to 0.61); a sandwich or negative binomial restores it. A structural-zero fraction that differs between source and target biases the transported absolute rate in every count model, including zero-inflated Poisson, by up to 0.56 on the log scale; the rate ratio is protected only without effect modification. Recalibrating the zero part to the target's reported zero proportion repairs the absolute rate when the source has structural zeros to learn from.

**What it does not answer.** One covariate; frailty, exposure weighting, recurrent events and zero-inflated negative binomial not run. Peer review has not been done.

### [OUT-14](problems/OUT-14-pseudo-ipd-cannot-express-delayed-entry-or-assessment-window.qmd) — Assessment grids that differ between trials

**Question.** When two trials assess progression on different visit schedules, how much does treating recorded event times as exact bias a transported RMST difference, and do midpoint imputation or an interval-censored model remove it?

**Answer.** Treating visit-recorded event times as exact biases a cross-trial RMST difference by half the spacing times the event probability by the horizon, with the sign set by which trial visits less often. A 3-month difference in spacing produced a spurious difference of 1.4 months with no true effect, and removed 1.0 of a true 1.2 months in another scenario. Moving events to the interval midpoint or fitting an interval-censored model reduced the bias below 0.1 month.

**What it does not answer.** Binary event-by-time endpoints, different maximum follow-up, reconstruction error from digitized curves and visit-window jitter were not simulated. Peer review has not been done.

### [OVL-01](problems/OVL-01-weak-overlap-leaves-target-regions-the-source-data-cannot-su.qmd) — Unsupported target mass matters only where the effect is modified

Also bears on [OVL-03](problems/OVL-03-no-support-diagnostic-aggregates-over-a-paic-target-distribu.qmd).

**Question.** When part of the target population lies outside the source trial's support, do weight and covariate diagnostics identify the analyses that fail, or is the modification in the unsupported region, which they cannot see, what decides it?

**Answer.** Unsupported target mass caused bias only where the effect bent in the unsupported direction (up to 0.29 for G-computation and 0.30 for MAIC with 27% of the target unsupported), and none with linear modification or orthogonal alignment. Weight and covariate diagnostics, identical across those scenarios by construction, discriminated failed analyses at chance within an overlap level (AUROC 0.48 to 0.52). An outcome-informed score reached 0.59 to 0.66, missing the registered margin by 0.01; neither was usable. Trimming to the supported region was unbiased for the restricted estimand.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome, two covariates; ML-NMR, ML-UMR and NMI not run; failure defined by non-coverage. Peer review has not been done.

### [OVL-02](problems/OVL-02-ess-is-an-insufficient-overlap-diagnostic-and-no-battery-is-.qmd) — An infeasible MAIC is signaled by its own balance table, not by its effective sample size

**Question.** MAIC has no solution when the target mean lies outside the convex hull of the source covariates. Does the optimizer say so, and can ESS, the maximum weight or the residual balance tell infeasible analyses from hard feasible ones?

**Answer.** The residual imbalance of the returned weights does, almost perfectly: above 0.001 in 99.9% of infeasible and 0.1% of feasible analyses. The optimizer reported convergence on 17% of infeasible problems. ESS ranks analyses well but the conventional rule of ESS below 10% of n flagged 73% of feasible analyses near the hull boundary as well as every infeasible one, so it cannot separate impossible from hard; and hard feasible analyses near the boundary undercovered badly anyway.

**What it does not answer.** Only feasibility of the mean constraint; support for the target joint law cannot be checked from published marginals. Normal covariates, MAIC on means, one sample size; the proposed diagnostics' computability taxonomy was not simulated. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/OVL-02-feasibility-and-what-published-data-can-compute/out/OVL-02.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/OVL-02-feasibility-and-what-published-data-can-compute/out/OVL-02.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/OVL-02-feasibility-and-what-published-data-can-compute/out/OVL-02.odt)

### [OVL-06](problems/OVL-06-no-standardized-sample-size-planning-guidance-or-software-fo.qmd) — Planning a MAIC from the estimator's influence function, not from n or Kish ESS

**Question.** Before any data exist, which planning quantity predicts the precision a MAIC will achieve: nominal sample size, Kish effective sample size, or the estimator's influence-function variance evaluated at posited source and target laws?

**Answer.** The influence-function variance. It predicted the achieved SD within 10% in 85% of 72 scenarios, missing only at 150 patients with 10% prevalence. Kish ESS was within 10% in 58% and understated the achieved SD in 99% of scenarios, so it is optimistic, not the conservative quantity it is usually taken to be; nominal n was within 10% in 21%.

**What it does not answer.** The planner is assumed to know the source and target laws. Binary outcome, anchored-side precision and MAIC on means only; the unanchored bias floor and survival outcomes are not run. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/OVL-06-planning-in-information-rather-than-in-n/out/OVL-06.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/OVL-06-planning-in-information-rather-than-in-n/out/OVL-06.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/OVL-06-planning-in-information-rather-than-in-n/out/OVL-06.odt)

### [QBA-06](problems/QBA-06-measurement-and-misclassification-qba-under-population-adjus.qmd) — A misclassified covariate that is both balanced and a modifier

**Question.** When a binary effect modifier is misclassified in the source, the target or both, which corrections does population adjustment need, and is correcting the outcome model alone enough?

**Answer.** No. MAIC on a misclassified binary modifier was biased even with identical assays in both studies (-0.03 to -0.13 on the log odds ratio scale), because reweighting recorded categories leaves each category's true composition at the source's; correcting the target prevalence alone did not help. Correcting only STC's outcome model left bias of -0.012 to -0.051. Fully corrected STC and MAIC with weights chosen on the latent prevalence were unbiased (within 0.006).

**What it does not answer.** Known assay parameters; one binary covariate; no interval assessment. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-06-an-error-that-enters-twice/out/QBA-06.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-06-an-error-that-enters-twice/out/QBA-06.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-06-an-error-that-enters-twice/out/QBA-06.odt)

### [QBA-07](problems/QBA-07-outcome-ascertainment-and-the-observation-process-in-externa.qmd) — Outcome ascertainment in an external comparator

**Question.** Does an interval-censored analysis cover the ascertainment differences between a trial and a routine-care comparator, or do missed detections and risk-dependent visiting still bias the RMST contrast?

**Answer.** Partly. With every progression detected, an interval-censored model removed the bias from the external arm's sparser visits (within 0.05 months) and was not biased by visits that depended on patients' risk at the strength simulated. When the external arm missed progression at some visits, every method was biased, by 0.25 to 0.38 months at a per-visit sensitivity of 0.85 and 0.67 to 0.94 at 0.7, against a true difference of 1.59 months. Missed detection needs its own bias parameter.

**What it does not answer.** No lag, linkage loss or false positives; one frailty and visiting strength; no sensitivity analysis over the detection parameter; no population adjustment. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-07-invoking-only-the-parameters-the-setting-warrants/out/QBA-07.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-07-invoking-only-the-parameters-the-setting-warrants/out/QBA-07.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-07-invoking-only-the-parameters-the-setting-warrants/out/QBA-07.odt)

### [QBA-11](problems/QBA-11-outcome-model-misspecification-and-doubly-robust-qba.qmd) — Which failures double robustness covers

**Question.** Does a doubly robust MAIC protect against an omitted confounder, and what happens to a sensitivity grid built on a misspecified outcome model?

**Answer.** Double robustness protects against one misspecified nuisance model and nothing else. With an omitted confounder the augmented estimator carried exactly the same bias as correctly specified weighting or outcome-regression estimators, and with both models wrong the misspecification and omitted-variable biases added. A sensitivity grid built on a misspecified analysis is therefore shifted by the misspecification bias. With exact-balance weights, augmentation by an outcome model built from the balanced terms reproduces MAIC.

**What it does not answer.** Continuous outcome only; no cross-fitting; drMAIC E-value screen and a formally bias-indexed doubly robust estimator not run. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-11-what-double-robustness-does-not-cover/out/QBA-11.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-11-what-double-robustness-does-not-cover/out/QBA-11.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-11-what-double-robustness-does-not-cover/out/QBA-11.odt)

### [QBA-13](problems/QBA-13-simulated-covariate-qba-is-an-stc-route-not-a-general-soluti.qmd) — A simulated-covariate bias analysis by STC and by MAIC

**Question.** Is a MAIC version of the simulated-covariate bias analysis infeasible or too imprecise, as its authors assumed when restricting it to STC?

**Answer.** The MAIC extension of the simulated-covariate bias analysis was feasible in at least 99.8% of replicates across assumed target prevalences from 0.1 to 0.9, lost effective sample size to 85 to 109 of 300 only at the extreme, and had a reported SE 3% to 14% above STC's. Both routes were unbiased. The restriction to STC was conservative rather than necessary. Both routes' multiply imputed intervals widened along the sweep more than the estimate's real spread (SE up to 0.28 against about 0.13), so coverage exceeded nominal.

**What it does not answer.** One binary unmeasured covariate, correct assumed relations, unanchored A side only, no decision reading. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-13-testing-the-reason-maic-was-excluded/out/QBA-13.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-13-testing-the-reason-maic-was-excluded/out/QBA-13.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-13-testing-the-reason-maic-was-excluded/out/QBA-13.odt)

### [QBA-20](problems/QBA-20-component-paic-needs-joint-population-and-bridge-bias-analys.qmd) — One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis of two bias layers reports robustness that the joint analysis does not support

**Question.** Do one-at-a-time sensitivity analyses of population transportability and component invariance bound their joint effect on a cross-gap contrast, or can the layers offset and report spurious robustness?

**Answer.** No. With an omitted modifier (population layer) and component drift (bridge layer) acting on one cross-gap log odds ratio of -0.20, each one-at-a-time curve stayed within 0.16 and never reversed the decision, while the joint elicited box reached a bias of -0.41 and 7% of it reversed the decision; 23% to 26% of the box lay outside the one-at-a-time envelope at every scale. Component-by-modifier drift, which current tooling excludes, moved the estimate by 0.04 alone because it acts through its product with the modifier imbalance.

**What it does not answer.** Population-level calculation on one logistic model; no sampling, component network fit or survival scale; joint covariate law known, so the cost of eliciting it is not measured; component non-additivity and backbone interactions not included. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-20-two-unidentified-layers-that-can-offset/out/QBA-20.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-20-two-unidentified-layers-that-can-offset/out/QBA-20.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-20-two-unidentified-layers-that-can-offset/out/QBA-20.odt)

### [QBA-23](problems/QBA-23-propagating-every-uncertainty-layer-without-prohibitive-cost.qmd) — Bootstrap intervals over a bias grid when resamples fail

**Question.** When a bootstrap sensitivity analysis drops resamples whose weights fail near the edge of support, how does the interval behave, and is conditioning on success immaterial?

**Answer.** No. Near the edge of the source's support, up to 67% of bootstrap resamples failed to produce MAIC weights, and the percentile interval from the survivors covered only 0.29 to 0.65 (0.14 to 0.56 counting failed original fits as giving no interval). The surviving resamples are those that contain the few patients who make the weights possible, so their spread understates the estimate's. The failure share should be reported as a result and the interval withheld where it is material.

**What it does not answer.** One covariate, continuous outcome; cost and surrogate approaches and identified sets not studied. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-23-an-interval-conditional-on-the-weighting-having-worked/out/QBA-23.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-23-an-interval-conditional-on-the-weighting-having-worked/out/QBA-23.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-23-an-interval-conditional-on-the-weighting-having-worked/out/QBA-23.odt)

### [QBA-24](problems/QBA-24-survival-qba-beyond-the-hazard-ratio-with-limited-aggregate-.qmd) — Does a hazard-scale bias translate proportionally into RMST?

**Question.** Can a sensitivity analysis stated as a hazard-ratio bias be reinterpreted as a proportional bias in RMST, the quantity the decision uses?

**Answer.** No. The RMST change caused by a hazard-scale bias depends on the baseline hazard's shape and the event level: at the same survival by 24 months the same bias moved RMST up to 1.44 times as much for a decreasing as for an increasing hazard, and the proportional (first-order) reinterpretation understated the change by about 25% with few events and overstated it by up to 8% with many. A hazard-ratio sensitivity analysis must be translated with the baseline curve or stated on the RMST scale.

**What it does not answer.** Only the hazard-to-RMST translation; the PAIC layer, pseudo-IPD and curve-based arms, reconstruction error and tipping sets not run. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-24-bias-parameterized-on-the-scale-the-decision-uses/out/QBA-24.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-24-bias-parameterized-on-the-scale-the-decision-uses/out/QBA-24.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-24-bias-parameterized-on-the-scale-the-decision-uses/out/QBA-24.odt)

### [QBA-26](problems/QBA-26-benchmarking-and-negative-controls-as-data-based-calibration.qmd) — A single-covariate benchmark against omitted composite structure

**Question.** Does the bias from dropping the strongest measured covariate bound the residual bias from several omitted variables, and does a scaled benchmark calibrate?

**Answer.** No. With three or six omitted variables each no stronger than the strongest measured covariate, the leave-one-covariate-out benchmark covered the true residual bias in at most 7% of analyses, the bias being 1.4 to 5.7 times the benchmark. Scaling by the square root of the number of omitted variables did not fix it; scaling by the number itself did when each omitted variable was weaker than the strongest measured one. The benchmark also shrank as omitted structure grew, through odds-ratio non-collapsibility.

**What it does not answer.** Omitted variables shifted in the same direction; one overlap level; negative-control route not run. Peer review has not been done.

Read it: [PDF](/studies/QBA-26-a-benchmark-that-cannot-reach-what-it-is-asked-about/out/QBA-26.pdf) · [Markdown](/studies/QBA-26-a-benchmark-that-cannot-reach-what-it-is-asked-about/out/QBA-26.md) · [OpenDocument](/studies/QBA-26-a-benchmark-that-cannot-reach-what-it-is-asked-about/out/QBA-26.odt)

### [SFW-10](problems/SFW-10-maicplus-variance-trimming-and-estimand-disclosure-gaps.qmd) — Stacking the weighting step into the MAIC sandwich makes intervals narrower, not better

**Question.** Does a stacked sandwich that accounts for weight estimation give better MAIC intervals than the fixed-weight sandwich or the ESS-based conventional variance, and what population does a trimmed MAIC actually estimate?

**Answer.** No. Stacking lowered the standard error in every untrimmed scenario (by up to 11%), because estimating calibration weights removes outcome variation the covariates explain; where MAIC intervals already undercover, at poor overlap, that made them worse (coverage down to 0.844). The fixed-weight sandwich was in band in 24 of 30 scenarios, the ESS-based variance in 18 and the stacked sandwich in 17, so current guidance stands. Trimming moved the estimand by up to 0.19 on the log odds ratio scale.

**What it does not answer.** No bootstrap and one sample size, so where stacking's asymptotic advantage appears is not located. Binary outcome, three covariates, MAIC on means. Peer review has not been done.

### [SFW-14](problems/SFW-14-drmaic-has-no-methods-paper-and-no-independent-evaluation.qmd) — drMAIC 0.1.0 returns the MAIC estimate as its doubly robust estimate, with an interval six times too narrow

**Question.** Does drMAIC 0.1.0 implement a doubly robust MAIC with valid intervals: is its augmented estimate robust to a wrong weighting model when the outcome model is right, and do its intervals cover?

**Answer.** No. drMAIC 0.1.0 averages the outcome model over the individual-data patients instead of the target population, so its doubly robust estimate equals its MAIC estimate in every replicate (difference below 2e-15) and keeps MAIC's bias when the weights are wrong and the outcome model right (0.066 against 0.004 for correct augmentation). Its analytic SE divides by n twice and mixes probability and log odds scales: 0.028 against an empirical SD of 0.17 to 0.22, coverage 0.20 to 0.26. Its percentile bootstrap covers 0.78 to 0.79.

**What it does not answer.** One package version, binary outcome, one sample size; G-MAIC not run; the time-to-event path (a weighted median labeled a hazard ratio) read from code, not simulated. Peer review has not been done.

## How a problem gets chosen

Not every open problem can be settled by a study, and the difference is not cosmetic.
A simulation can measure bias, coverage and error rates, and it can show how badly a
known nonidentification bites at realistic sample sizes. It cannot establish that a
package is missing, that clinicians misread a plot, that a field under-reports
something, or that a quantity is unidentifiable in principle. Those need software, a
case study, a meta-research corpus, or a proof.

Every one of the 336 catalog entries was judged on both questions separately,
by an external model, before the program started: is this a population-adjustment
problem, and what kind of study would settle it. The queue below is the intersection.

::: {.table-scroll}

| Why an entry is not in the program | n |
|---|---:|
| not a population-adjustment problem | 101 |
| needs analytic, not a simulation or case study | 69 |
| needs software, not a simulation or case study | 22 |
| needs consensus, not a simulation or case study | 17 |
| needs corpus, not a simulation or case study | 16 |
| needs none, not a simulation or case study | 1 |

:::

a study that turns out to answer two entries closes both, and a study whose design
review finds it would answer a neighbouring question rather than the stated one gets

## What each study has to do

Simulation studies follow ADEMP: aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods,
performance measures ([Morris, White and Crowther 2019](https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.8086)).
Two rules follow from it and are enforced rather than encouraged.

Every performance measure carries a Monte Carlo standard error.
:   A bias of 0.02 is uninterpretable without knowing whether the Monte Carlo error is
    0.001 or 0.03. The replicate count is derived in the protocol from a target Monte
    Carlo standard error, not chosen because it is a round number.

Failed replicates are results.
:   A method that converges on 60% of replicates and is unbiased on those is not an
    unbiased method. Convergence is reported for every method in every scenario.

The protocol is committed before the run.
:   It fixes the design and states in advance what result would count as showing the
    problem is real and what would count as showing it is not. The commit that adds it
    is the timestamp.

Code, protocols and results are at
[github.com/choxos/ITC-open-problems/tree/main/studies](https://github.com/choxos/ITC-open-problems/tree/main/studies).
